data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's system contains a performative contradiction: the rule 'prefer the better-corroborated theory' is itself a universal norm derived from the observed success of such preferences in the history of science, thereby employing the very inductive generalization it forbids.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the rule is justified transcendently (as a condition for the possibility of rational discourse) rather than empirically, the contradiction vanishes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'success' of the strategy is defined tautologically (survival = success), the induction is circular but not empirical.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Popper might argue the rule is a proposal, not a derived truth, escaping the need for justification.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The meta-rule of critical rationalism ('always choose the most tested theory') appears to be justified by the historical observation that this strategy works better than guessing. If this observation is the basis for the rule, then the rule is inductively derived. If the rule is not inductively derived, it is an arbitrary dogma. Thus, Popper either smuggles induction in at the meta-level or offers no reason to follow his methodology.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
